articles.title: 5 Biggest Questions Ahead of Valkyries vs. Dream WNBA Finals
articles.summary: The 2026 WNBA Finals are almost here, with the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream set to face off in what should be an all-time defensive matchup.
articles.body:
The 2026 WNBA Finals are almost here, with the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream set to face off in what should be an all-time defensive matchup.

Both teams have elite on-ball defenders in the backcourt, tons of versatility on the wing and are anchored by two of the best interior defenders in the league. Some of these games could be super low scoring, but the physicality and athleticism will be absolutely unbelievable.

The Valkyries swept the Dream in the regular season, but all three games came before the All-Star break, and Atlanta has looked like a much different team since then.

With that said, let's dive into our five biggest questions heading into the WNBA Finals.

How Will Allisha Gray Look Returning from Injury?

Allisha Gray's status heading into Game 1 is easily the biggest question of this series. She's listed as day-to-day after undergoing a minor procedure on her shooting hand following an injury early in Game 1 of the semifinals against New York.

Gray's had nearly two weeks to recover and has returned to shooting, so it would be a surprise if she doesn't give it a go. But even if she plays, how much will the injury affect her shot?

If Gray is healthy and shooting over 35 percent from three, that changes the game for the Dream. Atlanta can still win this series if she isn't, but it would put even more pressure on Rhyne Howard, who shot just 29.2 percent from three in the series against New York.

In a lot of ways, Atlanta and Golden State are similar teams. They're both elite defensive squads with a ton of athletes across all positions. But the way they go about things offensively is very different.

Atlanta played at the second-fastest pace among playoff teams during the regular season and thrives off creating turnovers and getting out in transition. Golden State, meanwhile, played at the slowest pace in the league and does an excellent job taking care of the ball, allowing just 11.7 points off turnovers this season.

Can the Dream force the Valkyries into mistakes and speed the game up, or can the Valkyries control the tempo and limit Atlanta's transition opportunities? That push and pull will be one of the biggest things to monitor throughout the series.

In the regular season, there's no question Golden State won this battle. The Valkyries went 3-0 against Atlanta and completely shut down the Dream's half-court offense. When they weren't in transition, Atlanta struggled to generate anything.

In those matchups, the Dream shot just 37.7 percent at the rim in the half-court and 30.6 percent in the half-court overall, per Synergy Sports.

Kiah Stokes was a force as a rim protector, Gabby Williams made life difficult on the wing and Veronica Burton set the tone at the point of attack.

However, all three games came before the All-Star break, and Atlanta's offense has been much better since then, particularly Angel Reese. Since the break, she has shot 52.4 percent at the rim in the half court—an 8.2 percentage-point increase from before it.

Is Gabby Williams' Scoring Run Sustainable?

Williams enters the Finals playing the best basketball of her career. Her 136 points through six playoff games are the most she's ever scored over any six-game stretch, according to Across the Timeline . She's also shooting 47.7 percent from two and 40.5 percent from three.

Williams is knocking down pull-up jumpers at a high rate, creating downhill as a driver and doing it all while rarely turning the ball over.

There's a chance this run continues, but what happens if her efficiency comes back down to earth against a much tougher perimeter defense than she faced in the first two rounds against Dallas and Las Vegas?

Williams has accounted for more than half of Golden State's points on pull-up jumpers this postseason. If she cools off, especially with Howard guarding her, the Valkyries just don't have anywhere near as much creation as the Dream.

Though, this is a team that can win games in the 60s and 70s, so it may not be an issue that keeps them from winning the series.

Is Jordin Canada's Scoring Run Sustainable?

Jordin Canada is also playing the best basketball of her career, turning into an offensive dynamo this postseason, particularly in the series against New York.

If you told people Canada would be Atlanta's best offensive player over a five-game stretch in the playoffs, nobody would've believed you.

She's been a major problem for opponents defensively (on and off the ball) and has turned that disruption into tons of transition opportunities as a scorer and passer.

On top of that, she's shooting 12-of-24 from three this postseason, including multiple pull-up threes after going just 6-of-36 off the dribble from beyond the arc during the regular season.

But this will be Canada's toughest matchup yet against Burton and Golden State. She was able to get by Sabrina Ionescu, Marine Fauthoux and Pauline Astier seemingly at will in the semifinals. That won't be as easy against the best point guard defender in the league and a player who takes care of the ball as well as Burton.

What If the Threes Stop Falling for the Valkyries?

Golden State is a team that lives and dies by the three, and that strategy has worked out beautifully. When they miss, they can often make up for it by grabbing their own rebounds and scoring or drawing fouls.

Golden State posted a 38.7 percent offensive rebound rate against Las Vegas, with their 41 offensive rebounds being tied for the fourth-most over a three-game playoff stretch since 2020.

The Aces were a mediocre defensive rebounding team all season, and the Valkyries took full advantage, thanks to Kayla Thornton, Kaila Charles and Kiah Stokes.

However, the Dream have the greatest rebounder in WNBA history in Reese and more athleticism across the floor, which will inherently make those second-chance opportunities harder to come by.

So if Golden State isn't hitting threes and can't generate as many extra possessions on the offensive glass, where does their offense come from? That's a major question heading into the series.

articles.title: Ranking the Top 30 NBA Creators Ahead of 2026-27
articles.summary: Debating top-10-star status has become a rite of passage for NBA fandom.
articles.body:
Debating top-10-star status has become a rite of passage for NBA fandom.

But why stop there? Heading into the 2026-27 season, the B/R NBA staff is ready to litigate who's who among the Association's best—not only from an all-around perspective but also in several skill categories.

As in seasons past, we're not predicting where players will finish in April. This is a breakdown of where the league stands right now, meaning players set to start the year sidelined or unsigned aren't included.

Giannis Antetokounmpo has led the league in free-throw attempts four times and two-point field goals three times. The same hard-charging style that produced those results also allows him to spray the ball out to shooters.

For years, defenders have tried to combat Giannis' long strides, whirlwind spins and bruising shoulder checks by building a wall. Because it takes multiple bodies to do that, some number of Antetokounmpo's teammates get left unattended. So although Giannis isn't some preternatural passer who sees events before they happen, the net effect of his scoring aggression makes him a great facilitator.

All he has to do is scare opponents into filling up the lane, and he's got his choice of kick-out options.

Nobody who watched Scottie Barnes average 8.6 assists across seven postseason games against the Cleveland Cavaliers last spring needs to hear this, but the Toronto Raptors' do-it-all forward can pass the rock.

Barnes' size, length and athleticism allow him to carve out space, draw defenders and capitalize on a collapsing defense. Though his handle isn't that of a conventional guard, his 6'8" stature and forceful style make it very difficult for opponents to disrupt him on the ball.

One of Toronto's issues last season was a lack of shooting. If the Raps had surrounded Barnes with more spacing threats, his 5.9 assists per game would have checked in a lot closer to his 9.6 potential assists per game. It only goes down as a dime in the box score if your teammate can knock down the shot.

The Orlando Magic offense has never been known for its ball movement, and Jalen Suggs tends to play so hard on defense that his minutes can't safely be allowed to climb too high. Both facts, neither of which actually speak to Suggs' skills, are beyond his control.

We know Suggs can pass because he averaged 9.5 dimes per 100 possessions last season, despite occupying nothing more than a third-option role whenever the Magic were healthy.

BBall Index rates his playmaking talent and passing creation quality as A-plusses , and Suggs also ranks in the 90th percentile in assist points created per 75 possessions. In other words, he's an extremely capable creator who doesn't get the rep count to amass conventional stats to prove it.

There's no way Austin Reaves would have gotten his $180 million contract in July if he were only being paid as a scorer.

Though he could only show it when Luka Dončić and/or LeBron James were out of the lineup last season, Reaves is an adept playmaker whose shifty handle and craft in the lane allow him to make plays like a true point guard.

Whether he's putting the ball exactly where it needs to be in transition or scanning the floor with eyes that seem to be in the back of his head , Reaves is a gifted bucket-getter who maps the court as if the goal is always to find an open teammate.

Get ready for Darius Garland to climb these rankings, as he's about to step back into the primary creation role that allowed him to rack up 8.6 assists per game back in 2021-22.

Donovan Mitchell's arrival in Cleveland the following season naturally took the ball out of Garland's hands, which makes the 7.8 assists he averaged that year all the more impressive. As the Cavs moved forward, though, Garland's elite three-point shooting became a bigger weapon than his passing.

Now running the show with the LA Clippers, a new career high in assists feels likely. Garland could get there by running more pick-and-rolls and becoming the every-possession outlet in transition.

25. Stephen Curry, Golden State Warriors

Any possession that ends with Stephen Curry shooting the basketball is a good one, but the greatest marksman of all time has also done plenty of damage by capitalizing on every defense's fear of his stroke.

When all five defenders scramble to keep you from shooting, it creates an array of passing options to teammates who are typically open.

Curry has only averaged more than 8.0 assists per game once and generally finishes seasons closer to 6.0. That's not because he's anything less than one of the smartest passers and best ball-handlers in the league, but instead because no rationally devised offense would see him sacrifice any more of his own scoring chances than that.

Draymond Green is largely viewed as Golden State's main facilitator, but Curry has over 1,300 more career assists.

24. Draymond Green, Golden State Warriors

Draymond Green overcame his limitations as a shooter by becoming one of the greatest defensive players of all time. If he hadn't also developed into an elite passer, he might still have struggled to play such a significant role in four championship seasons.

It turns out that building your whole offensive game around passing the ball to Stephen Curry and Klay Thompson is a pretty good idea.

Green figured out that cheat code in 2015-16, when he logged what remains a career-high 598 assists. A whopping 161 set up Thompson, while 159 of them went to Curry.

After Golden State lost Kevin Durant and Thompson, Green honed a handoff and hot-potato two-man game with Steph that flummoxed defenses and effectively functioned as the Golden State Warriors' go-to scoring plan whenever things got tight.

Green, Nikola Jokic and LeBron James are the only non-point guards to rank in the top 10 in total assists since 2015-16.

The athleticism may be waning, and availability has been an issue, but Ja Morant has never lost his ability to distribute the basketball.

Even last year, when his scoring efficiency truly abandoned him in 20 underwhelming appearances, Morant matched a career high with 8.1 assists per game and averaged 4.8 rim assists per game —ahead of James Harden and LeBron James.

At his absolute peak, Morant was capable of ball-handling tricks no one this side of Kyrie Irving could even imagine. Quick, creative and highly aggressive, Morant could get to any spot on the floor in a blink.

It remains to be seen if Morant can continue to make that kind of impact on a Blazers roster that doesn't seem built for his skill set, but he'll find open teammates often enough if he can get into space and attract help defense.

Deni Avdija's downhill prowess is the key to his status as one of the league's best emerging distributors. Using his heft, an elite slow-down Eurostep and the occasional off-arm shove, Avdija amassed a league-high 4.9 free-throw attempts per game on an NBA-best 27.8 drives per game .

More than a head-down attacker, Avdija passed out of his drives 53.2 percent of the time and also led the league with 3.1 assists per game on drives.

Just imagine how much higher that number might have been if the Portland Trail Blazers had surrounded him with more willing shooters.

Like a lot of the rest of his game, Alperen Sengün's passing is effective because of how he weaponizes awkwardness. Sengün shoots off the wrong foot constantly, takes strange angles and generally operates at a cadence that causes confusion in his opponents.

That means his setups come at unusual times and from unexpected spots. He'll catch defenders unawares with a behind-the-back bouncer when he burrows into the post, and he's no stranger to the old "fake spin move before a no-look, two-hand shovel" if a teammate cuts at the right time.

Patient enough to pivot three or four times on a single touch, Sengün sometimes just waits out defenders. When they relax, he continues the action and usually finds somebody for an open look.

Kyrie Irving's creation starts with arguably the best handle of all time. Gifted with a singular ability to get to any spot on the floor with a live dribble, Irving commands uncommon levels of attention when he has the ball.

Scoring is always his first instinct, which it should be. Anyone who can so effectively work his way into space and then attack with one of the most diverse and creative finishing packages of all time would be doing fans a disservice if he didn't try to convert on his own. But Irving also has a knack for finding teammates in ways that clearly catch defenders off guard.

Here's a personal favorite from a few years ago.

With apologies to Domantas Sabonis, De'Aaron Fox was the most important creator on the 2022-23 Sacramento Kings who, at the time, set the record for offensive efficiency in a season.

That version of Fox still possessed his league-best open-floor speed and had gained enough experience to maximize its impact. Almost no one was more dangerous in transition or turning the corner on a handoff, and Fox used his physical advantages to set up others as often as he scored himself.

A half-step slower and now playing a less central role for the San Antonio Spurs, Fox can still turn on the jets and sling passes to the corners with the best of them. Better still, he's grown more careful with the ball over the years. Last season saw Fox set a new career low with just 3.5 turnovers per 100 possessions.

Only four players have averaged at least 25.0 points and 5.0 assists per game in each of the last four seasons, and Devin Booker is one of them .

The Phoenix Suns' mid-range maestro is a scorer first, but the team's roster construction has often cast Booker in the role of primary creator. That's probably too much responsibility for someone who is also required to rack up first-option scoring numbers, but it's impressive that the 11-year vet continues to answer the call.

The threat of Booker's pull-up mid-ranger means his individual defender has to stay close and helpers have to slide his way when he gets into the upper paint. He uses that gravity to fire pocket passes to rollers and flick lobs to cutters on the baseline.

17. Donovan Mitchell, Cleveland Cavaliers

Donovan Mitchell's seven straight years of at least 24.0 points per game mark him as a score-first player, but he's learned to leverage the threat of his own offense to create chances for teammates.

The best illustration of that came back in 2023, when Mitchell scored a career-high 71 points but also handed out 11 assists against the Chicago Bulls. No one with a scoring total that high had ever logged double-digit dimes , and no one's done it since.

When defenses have to honor a scorer at all three levels, and when that scorer is also willing to swing the ball at the right time, great offense is basically a given.

Speed puts pressure on a defense, contracting it and opening up passing options elsewhere on the floor. Tyrese Maxey, one of the fastest players in the league, has been using his velocity to create scoring chances for others since he entered the league in 2020-21.

Though tasked mainly with scoring the last handful of years, Maxey has averaged at least 6.1 assists per game every season since 2023-24. His ability to bend defenses with his quickness shows up in the way he puts teammates in position to reach the foul line.

Because Maxey's burst and handle draw so much attention, cutters can slip into vulnerable spaces, receive a pass and attack compromised defenders. Only five players hit shooters who were immediately fouled more often than Maxey.

This'll sound meaner than most compliments do, but Isaiah Collier is in the league because of his playmaking.

Without the setup skills that allowed him to average 9.3 assists per 36 minutes over his first two seasons, the ruggedly strong point guard's shooting (25.7 percent from three) and suspect defense wouldn't have been nearly enough to earn him rotation minutes and 65 starts.

Collier's on-ball abilities make him the central part of the Utah Jazz's offense whenever he's in the game.

Last season, only two players—Josh Giddey and TJ McConnell—accounted for a higher share of their team's assists when on the floor (minimum 50 games played). Given his youth and the gains he could unlock by becoming a more dangerous perimeter threat, Collier has a better shot than most to climb these rankings.

Jalen Johnson blossomed into an All-NBA star last season, and a lot of his growth owed to the Atlanta Hawks putting the ball in his hands more as a playmaker. En route to a career-best 8.0 assists per game, the 24-year-old forward showcased a remarkably deep arsenal of passes.

Adept at fitting high-speed bouncers into tight windows in transition, capable of firing two-handers over the top of defenses to rolling bigs and especially gifted at finding the dunker when he gets into the paint, Johnson clearly sees the game like a point guard.

His assist rate last season slotted into the 98th percentile among forwards, marking Johnson as one of the absolute best high-volume creators at his position.

Often, players with high assist numbers get them by hanging onto the ball for longer than average while they hunt down angles and wait for teammates to get into prime scoring position. Josh Giddey does things a little differently.

In averaging 9.1 assists per game last year, Giddey only dribbled 3.1 times per touch . For context, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Jalen Brunson are right around 5.0 dribbles per touch; LaMelo Ball and Cade Cunningham are usually around 4.5. Further evidence that the ball rarely sticks with Giddey: He averaged 71.7 passes per game in 2025-26, a figure topped only by Jokić.

We tend to spend a lot of time picking nits with Giddey. He's not much of a defender, and defenses still aren't all that worried about him as a scoring threat. But the guy plays truly unselfish ball and involves his teammates better than almost anyone.

Sure, it's a little easier to create scoring chances when your most frequent partner in the two-man game is Nikola Jokić. But Jamal Murray isn't just out there racking up buckets and assists by accident.

Murray ranked 11th in the league last year in touches per game and fourth in secondary assists per game. In other words, he possessed the ball a ton, moved it without hunting his own assists and yet still managed to average a career-best 7.1 dimes per contest.

When Murray played without Jokić in 2025-26, that number climbed to 8.3 helpers per game.

While Jokić's impact is undeniably positive, Murray's facilitating stats are probably suppressed because he just happens to play with one of the best setup artists anyone's ever seen.

Though age has made him less of a threat to finish around the basket and therefore slightly more predictable for defenses, James Harden's pure skill and vision still make him one of the top playmakers around.

Starting with a handle that defenders still haven't figured out how to disrupt, Harden is able to get his shoulder past his man in isolation and read the floor in what feels like slow motion.

Lobs, spray-out lasers to the corners and slick over-the-shoulder finds to shooters waiting above the break are all on the menu. Much like LeBron, Harden has seen every coverage and knows where the cracks are. What he's lost in foot speed and scoring ability around the rim, he continues to make up for with his mental edge and experience.

LeBron James has led the league in assists just once and only averages 7.4 dimes per game for his career, but any serious examination of the history of basketball has to include him among the game's all-time great facilitators.

James sees the floor like few others, and his size has always allowed him access to passing angles—over the top, around outstretched arms, through traffic—most others miss.

With an encyclopedic knowledge of other teams' tendencies, more high-pressure minutes played than anyone in league history and hard wiring to play the right way, James' situational awareness and calm give him extra advantages that seem unfair in light of his physical tools and natural passing talents. He'll never be flustered by tricky coverage or defensive gimmicks. He's seen everything and can diagnose where the ball needs to go under any circumstances.

For 23 years, James has rated as an A-plus playmaker.

Overwhelming athleticism made more potent by a competitive mean streak makes Stephon Castle a nightmare to defend. And while opponents are simply trying not to get knocked into the basket stanchion or dunked over, the San Antonio Spurs point guard frequently catches them unaware by ending possessions with a setup rather than a score.

Per BBall Index's playmaking metrics, Castle grades out as an A-plus in playmaking talent, passing creation volume and passing creation quality. In other words, he doesn't just facilitate often. He does so with pinpoint looks that create extremely high-value scoring chances for others.

In his second season, Castle put up 8.9 assists per 36 minutes. Even with teammate Dylan Harper emerging and De'Aaron Fox still likely to possess the ball plenty, that figure feels like a floor going forward.

Jalen Brunson has never averaged more than 7.3 assists per game over a full season, but he still qualifies as an elite creator because of the other ways in which he generates offense for teammates.

Among players who logged at least 1,500 minutes, no player spent a larger percentage of his court time in possession of the basketball last season than Brunson, who had the rock a whopping 48.1 percent of the time he was in the game for the New York Knicks. His ability to probe the defense, threaten to score from anywhere and manipulate opponents freed up scoring chances for everyone else.

The sheer stamina it takes to play like Brunson is also a factor. His ability to dominate the ball and attract defensive attention for such large chunks of the game allows everyone else to cut hard, fire away from deep with fresh legs and otherwise maximize the looks Brunson creates.

7. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Oklahoma City Thunder

In his second straight MVP season last year, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander cemented himself as the toughest individual cover in the league. He dominated in isolation and ranked first in scoring efficiency among high-volume pick-and-roll ball-handlers, posting an incredible 1.2 points per possession in those sets.

Because he was (and is) such a threat to score or draw shooting fouls with the ball, SGA's setups became incredibly valuable. With defenses generally freaking out whenever he turned the corner or sized up his man in isolation, Gilgeous-Alexander's teammates found themselves in advantage situations all the time.

When Gilgeous-Alexander passed the ball, it produced an assist 17.3 percent of the time. No one who played over 20 games last year topped that assist-to-pass percentage.

It's still the right move to make SGA a passer because he's so hard to handle as a scorer, but his development as a setup man makes that a clear pick-your-poison situation.

If creative flair and a swashbuckling style were worth bonus points, LaMelo Ball would probably check in a few spots higher on our list. As it is, he's got the underlying individual and team numbers to clearly rate as an ace creator.

Last season, the Charlotte Hornets' offensive rating was 11.6 points per 100 possessions higher with Ball in the game, the second straight year that figure was north of 11.0. That on-off spike owes to Ball's inventive style in the half-court and his knack for slinging the ball ahead in transition.

Though a career average of just 7.3 assists per game might not seem impressive, it's important to note that Ball makes up for a relative lack of quantity with quality. Among players who averaged at least 20.0 potential assists per 100 possessions last season, Ball checked in behind only Nikola Jokić in a stat called "assist effective field-goal percentage," which measures how efficiently teammates converted on Ball's setups.

That means he generated an exceptionally high share of easy and open scoring opportunities. Anthony Edwards is going to have a blast this season.

The Detroit Pistons went out and got a whole bunch of shooting this past offseason, apparently convinced that more spacing is all it'll take to get their offense up to championship standards.

Critics (raises hand) might argue additional playmaking was the real need, to which the Pistons might reply: "We have Cade Cunningham, and he's enough."

Even with some pretty shoddy spacing last year, Cunningham ranked second only to Jokić with 24.8 points per game created via assist. Surround him with a couple more reliable shot-makers, and it stands to reason the Pistons will score plenty.

Cunningham has averaged at least 9.1 dimes per game in each of the last two years and should be able to use his size, handle, patience and vision to make it three in a row.

With three years averaging at least 10.0 assists per game and some of the best pick-and-roll timing anyone's ever seen, Trae Young grades out as one of the top setup artists of the past decade.

Normally, players with Young's relatively small stature are limited as passers. They get into the lane and can't see through or over the thicket of arms that closes in around them. Because he's such a threat to throw lobs and hit floaters, and because Young has a preternatural ability to map the floor ahead of time, he always finds a way to deliver the rock to an open teammate.

In 2024-25, Young's last healthy season, nobody generated more assists at the rim per 100 possessions.

Ball dominance defines Luka Dončić's offensive style, and he's basically spent his entire career in complete control of his team's possessions. That's why it's so interesting that he led all players (minimum 50 games) last season in secondary assists .

While it's true that Dončić racks up loads of conventional setups by making the pass that leads directly to a shot, his court mapping and anticipation skills also allow him to make the pass before the pass that creates a bucket.

Dončić has led the league in scoring twice, and he leverages the threat of his own offense better than almost anyone else. His individual matchup has to extend far up the floor in case Dončić goes to his patented step-back three, and every helper in the game shades in his direction. It's almost unfair that Dončić, using his size and vision, gets to take advantage of compromised defenders on almost every possession.

When we last saw him healthy, Tyrese Haliburton was a win away from finishing out one of the most breathtaking offensive seasons in memory with a championship.

Hali's captaincy of the 2024-25 Indiana Pacers produced one of the more magical offensive runs in years. Leading a fast-paced attack with his daredevil shotmaking and brilliant vision, Haliburton put himself into rarified air as a floor general.

Plenty of players can rack up assists, but Haliburton's offensive style was infectious in the best way. It called the likes of Steve Nash to mind, a player who won MVPs because he was always craftily hunting for the best angles and passing windows.

If Haliburton is back to himself following a season spent rehabbing his torn Achilles, he'll slot in behind only Jokić among the league's most captivating and transformative creators.

It's been years since there was any question whether Nikola Jokić is the best big-man passer in NBA history. He's blown past the other candidates—Bill Walton, Pau Gasol, Arvydas Sabonis, Vlade Divac—in career assists and, visually, has a much more diverse and creative setup package than any of them.

Those guys provided good value on offense with their creation skills. Jokić is different. He drives what is routinely the best offense in the league.

Last year's leader in assists per game, Jokić's court mapping and vision are unsurpassed by any of his current peers—regardless of position. His soft hands, anticipation and size allow him to see angles and execute passes nobody else can. His outlets, handoffs and no-look dimes are all equally perfect.

No one exercises complete control of the on-court proceedings like Jokić.

articles.title: In 2025, NBA star Deandre Ayton pledged $100,000 to rebuild his mother’s Jamaican hometown after Hurricane Melissa while helping over 1,500 kids chase basketball dreams through a free camp
articles.summary: Deandre Ayton is helping young people in Jamaica find opportunities through basketball, education and community support.
articles.body: Deandre Ayton is helping young people in Jamaica find opportunities through basketball, education and community support. The NBA center has joined forces with the PMBL Youth Basketball Camp in Treasure Beach, adding support to a programme that has spent more than a decade giving children access to the sport. His Ayton Family Foundation is also helping communities recover from Hurricane Melissa, bringing food, supplies and rebuilding assistance to families in his mother’s Jamaican hometown.The partnership offers a closer look at Ayton’s work away from the court. While the Phoenix-born basketball star has built his career in the NBA, his family’s Caribbean roots have shaped his charitable efforts. From providing equipment and meals to supporting damaged homes and community facilities, his foundation is working to make a difference that lasts beyond a single basketball season.Deandre Ayton joins Jamaica’s PMBL Youth Basketball Camp to support young playersThe PMBL Youth Basketball Camp began in 2013 through a partnership between four friends from the United States and Jamaican hotelier Jason Henzell. Henzell welcomed the group to Jake’s Hotel in Treasure Beach and gave them access to Breds Treasure Beach Sports Park, helping them bring their idea to life.The camp started with 35 children on its first day. By the end of that first week, attendance had grown to 225. Over the years, the programme has expanded its reach, offering children access to basketball, athletic equipment and other essentials.Per Sporting News, the camp now provides more than 1,500 children each year with items such as shoes, shirts, backpacks, hygiene products and school supplies. Individual donations and the volunteers’ personal networks have helped sustain the initiative.Ayton’s partnership with the camp adds another source of support. His Ayton Family Foundation works on youth development, food access and community programmes, with a focus on the Bahamas, Jamaica and Los Angeles. The foundation’s involvement also connects the camp to Ayton’s family ties in St. Elizabeth Parish, where his mother grew up.The partnership has a practical purpose. Children need more than a basketball court to take part in a sport. They also need equipment, food, transportation and a welcoming environment. The PMBL camp works to remove those barriers by keeping participation free and providing meals to campers.Children as young as four and as old as 18 can attend. The organisers focus on willingness to participate rather than skill level, giving beginners a chance to learn alongside more experienced players.The daily programme also goes beyond drills and matches. Coaches organise games and other activities for younger children, while the camp provides breakfast and lunch. Local restaurant Jack Sprat prepares meals, which often include jerk chicken with rice and peas.That mix of sport, food and community support gives the programme a broader purpose. It allows children to enjoy basketball without asking their families to cover the cost of a camp, equipment or daily meals. Ayton Family Foundation steps up after Hurricane MelissaAyton’s work in Jamaica took on greater urgency after Hurricane Melissa struck the island in October 2025. The storm caused severe damage in parts of St. Elizabeth Parish, the same region where his mother has family roots.In Dec. 2025, the NBA and the National Basketball Players Association recognised Ayton with the NBA Cares Bob Lanier Community Assist Award for November. The award highlighted his hurricane relief work in Jamaica and his efforts to improve food access and cultural inclusion among young people in LA. The NBA and NBPA Foundation also pledged $20,000 to the Ayton Family Foundation in recognition of his work.The foundation had already supported the reopening of the Cedar Spring Community Center in St. Elizabeth Parish in July 2025. The renovated facility now serves as a community space for education, health activities, recreation, youth programmes and family engagement.During the reopening, Ayton and the foundation hosted a community day for more than 100 children and families. The event offered free medical and dental screenings, school supplies, sneakers and a community meal.Following Hurricane Melissa, the foundation committed $100,000 towards rebuilding efforts and turned the Cedar Spring center into an emergency shelter and distribution hub. It also coordinated shipments of food and essential goods for affected residents.The rebuilding effort includes funding new zinc roofs for 30 families, along with financial support for longer-term recovery work planned for 2026. These steps address immediate needs while helping residents begin the difficult process of repairing their homes.The foundation’s involvement also reached the PMBL camp. The Ayton Family Foundation helped arrange transportation for children from areas hit hard by Hurricane Melissa, including Parrottee, Galleon and Black River.That support gives children from affected communities a chance to take part in camp activities despite the disruption caused by the storm. It also brings the foundation’s relief work and youth development efforts together in one programme.The camp itself has faced severe weather challenges before. After Hurricane Beryl hit the area in July 2024, volunteers cleared debris from the sports grounds and repaired damaged basketball facilities so the children could still attend a shortened camp. The experience showed how the programme could offer a sense of routine even when the community faced a difficult recovery. Why the Jamaica basketball project means more than a week of campThe PMBL partnership reflects a larger aim behind Ayton’s charitable work: making sport accessible while supporting the everyday needs of families.Basketball remains central to the camp, but the organisers also focus on access to food, school supplies and safe spaces. Those services can make a real difference for children whose families face financial pressure or are still recovering from a natural disaster.The camp also gives children a chance to meet coaches and volunteers who encourage them to learn, work with others and keep trying. It does not promise that every participant will become a professional player. Instead, it creates an environment where young people can enjoy the sport and develop their skills without worrying about the cost of joining.Ayton’s foundation follows a similar approach in its other programmes. In Los Angeles, it launched the Ayton Alley Oop Program, which provides tickets to Lakers games and other sporting events for young people from underrepresented communities. It has also worked with groups including the Boys & Girls Club, the Salvation Army and SüprMarkt LA on food access and cultural inclusion.In Dec. 2025, the NBA reported that Ayton had committed $25,000 to SüprMarkt LA’s SNAP BACK initiative, which provides fresh produce and healthy meals to families in need. The contribution reflects the foundation’s interest in addressing basic needs alongside opportunities for young people.Ayton explained that philosophy in a statement included in the NBA’s Dec. 17, 2025 announcement of his Community Assist Award. “My family taught me that feeding people is love,” he said, describing the values behind his foundation.Ayton’s NBA career puts him in a position to draw attention and resources to these efforts. articles.body: Evan Turner, el número 2 del Draft de 2010 que jugó en los Philadelphia 76ers de 2010 a 2014, cree que "a LeBron James (41 años) todavía le queda mucha cuerda". El exjugador de 37 años, que también trabajó como técnico asistente de los Boston Celtics, declaró que "a LeBron le quedan otros 5 ó 10 años al mismo nivel, igual que a Kevin Durant". "Es como si se preguntaran: '¿A dónde voy ahora?'. Ya no les queda nada más por hacer. ¡Esto es pan comido!", apuntó. Evan Turner sostiene que "creo que LeBron James jugará más de dos años. No está bajando el ritmo. Si nos fijamos en lo que ocurrió tras la primera serie de playoffs... eliminó a los Houston Rockets —que cuentan con un gran entrenador, Ime Udoka, y un gran talento joven, además de Kevin Durant y otros—, y logró llevar a su equipo a superar la primera ronda. Eso es algo sumamente difícil, especialmente cuando pierdes a tus dos mejores jugadores. Creo que todavía le queda mucha gasolina en el depósito". Sobre la posibilidad de que LeBron James gane un quinto anillo, lo que lo dejaría a uno solo de Michael Jordan, Turner señaló que no cree que James regrese si logra conquistar otro título: "Conociendo a LeBron, no estoy seguro de si volvería después de ganar otro anillo, a menos que él así lo quisiera. Ya dijo, tras vencer a los Warriors, que se considera el mejor jugador de todos los tiempos, y creo que realmente lo cree. Si analizamos los números y las estadísticas... bueno, yo soy de Chicago: para mí, Michael Jordan es el más grande de la historia (G.O.A.T.). Que no quepa duda. Pero al final, es algo personal. ¿Qué es suficiente? ¿Qué significa ser el mejor? Ha llegado a ocho finales consecutivas. ¿Entiendes a lo que me refiero? Ha logrado muchísimo. La gente no valorará lo que ha hecho hasta que ya no esté". "LeBron James ya consolidó su legado mucho antes de cumplir los 30 años. Todos dijimos: 'Vale, perfecto, su lugar en la historia ya está asegurado'. Lo tenemos claro: él no necesita ese trofeo. Llegó un punto en el que LeBron es, básicamente, el baloncesto mismo. Es increíble pensar que lleva jugando 30 años; es algo absolutamente asombroso. Pero agradezco todo lo que ha demostrado, el nivel que mantiene y el compromiso real que ha mostrado siempre", subrayó. Evan Turner destaca que el "superequipo" que son los LeBron James, que cuenta con estrellas de la talla de Tyrese Maxey, Jaylen Brown, LeBron James o Joel Embiid, ya es uno de los cinco mejores equipos de la NBA. "Los Sixers sin duda, son uno de los cinco mejores equipos, sólo por el talento que tienen. Poseen un talento increíble. También he visto algunos contenidos en los medios y me gusta cómo fluyen las cosas. Parece que LeBron está disfrutando de su estancia allí. Maxey sigue manteniendo esa misma sonrisa de siempre. Por lo poco que conozco a Jaylen Brown, su energía y su aura sugieren que también se lo está pasando bien. Me encanta lo que veo en sus cuatro figuras principales", compartió. Evan Turner cree que "a los Sixers les irá muy bien, siempre y cuando jueguen de la forma adecuada y afronten la temporada como deben. Si aspiras a llegar lejos en los playoffs y quieres ser un equipo campeón, necesitas cohesión. Debes conocer los detalles: con quién combinar mejor, qué estrategias funcionan y a quién recurrir en los momentos decisivos", continuó Turner. "Tienen que jugar al ajedrez, no a las damas, y garantizar que sus jugadores estén disponibles para los playoffs. Tomemos el caso de Joel Embiid. Me gustaría que jugara sólo unos 55 partidos al año y, con suerte, que en esos encuentros estuviera en cancha 28 minutos o menos. ¿Entiendes a lo que me refiero? Se trata de limitar sus minutos, pero asegurándose de que el equipo sepa cómo jugar con él en pista, pase lo que pase. Recuerdo la serie de playoffs contra los Celtics, donde él tuvo una actuación brillante; sin embargo, esa falta de preparación, de tiempo de juego y de química con el equipo —derivada de sus constantes lesiones— terminó pasando factura", recomendó.

articles.title: WNBA Finals: Golden State Valkyries begin quest for championship in second year of existence against Atlanta Dream
articles.summary: The Golden State Valkyries host the Atlanta Dream to start the WNBA Finals, live on Sky Sports Mix and Sky Sports+ from 8.30pm Saturday; Golden State went 3-0 against Atlanta during regular season, winning previous meeting 88-83 on July 4
articles.body:
This year's Finals, which begins on Saturday in San Francisco, brings together two franchises seeking their first WNBA titles.

Golden State became the first WNBA expansion team to qualify for the playoffs in their inaugural season in 2025 and followed that by reaching the Finals in only their second season, another expansion franchise record.

Valkyries owner Joe Lacob will walk into the Chase Center and feel the energy and vibe of the Valkyries' "Ballhalla" home crowd in what will be a violet-crazed sell-out.

Lacob promised a championship within the first five years and now in the second year the Valkyries are playing for one.

"What is truly remarkable is how great our fans are. Our players love it, we love it," Lacob said.

"It's great, it's a cohesion, it's everybody coming together all at the same time and rooting for something that is new and fresh and it's timely. And people see it and feel it. What's going on in that arena is fantastic; it's remarkable, it's incredibly fun.

"I love walking in there, my wife, my family, we all love walking in there to the tremendous feeling of camaraderie and togetherness.

"We all, as a team of people, fans, players, organisation - together we're making history, and we all feel it."

'We felt that we had something worth fighting for'

Under Lacob's leadership, Golden State has built a roster of understated stars under Natalie Nakase, who was hired as the first head coach for the Valkyries in October 2024.

Veronica Burton got cut by Dallas two years ago, while her back-up point guard Kaitlyn Chen was briefly let go by the Valkyries last season before she returned.

Kayla Thornton is a 33-year-old undrafted forward out of the University of Texas El Paso who became an All-Star in 2025.

Gabby Williams had something to prove in the WNBA after sensing others didn't believe in her ability.

"It feels special because this is a special group," Williams said. "All we need is each other.

"We just need to believe in each other. We know we weren't a team that was talked about, but just the culture and going to work every day.

"We felt that we had something worth fighting for. That's how we're going into the finals, with that same mentality - staying together and staying unselfish."

The Valkyries finished the 2026 regular season 32-12 before advancing through the playoffs, including a semi-final victory over defending champion Las Vegas Aces.

Atlanta, who have lost three previous Finals appearances in 2010, 2011 and 2013, are hoping to put the memory behind them to claim their first championship in franchise history.

articles.title: “Why am I not allowed to have a passion and a dream and a voice?”: Stephen Curry’s wife Ayesha Curry recalls facing backlash for pursuing her own career
articles.summary: Stephen Curry, the Golden State Warriors’ star player and his wife, Ayesha Curry, have built a pretty strong marriage in the last two decades.
articles.body: Stephen Curry, the Golden State Warriors’ star player and his wife, Ayesha Curry, have built a pretty strong marriage in the last two decades. While the four time NBA champion’s career has taken off, his wife, popular entrepreneur and chef, Ayesha Curry, never let it stop her from making a name for herself. Amid this, Stephen Curry’s wife Ayesha Curry reflects on the criticisms she faced.Stephen Curry’s wife Ayesha Curry opens up about how she was criticized for wanting her own career amid his successA few years ago, in an interview with the Working Mother, the popular actress Ayesha Curry reflected on her life as she said, “When my career was starting to take off, this male reporter bashed me on live television, saying I should be more like the other [basketball] players’ wives…”Stephen Curry’s wife Ayesha Curry added, “He literally said, ‘They sit there, they don’t cause any problems, and they look pretty.’”She continued, “Why am I not allowed to have a passion and a dream and a voice?” she continued. “That started a fire in me. I could not be stopped, and I wanted to prove myself. Now the conversation has shifted. Stephen doesn’t get any negative [questions] about me. Especially in the Bay Area, people say to him, ‘I like her food a lot,’ and that’s been special for me.”But that’s not all; over the last decade Ayesha Curry has faced a lot of hate for being outspoken about wanting to have a career of her own.While many of their fans saw her inspirational, others bashed her for her remarks.Stephen Curry stands by his wife Ayesha Curry as she experiences hate for her remarksFor the unversed, last year, Ayesha Curry opened up about how she wanted a career as a child and never saw herself getting married early or having children.These remarks sparked outrage among fans as many even urged the four time NBA champion and the Golden State Warriors’ star player Stephen Curry to seek a divorce.However, Stephen Curry stood by his wife’s side and defended her against all the hate she faced.In an interview, Stephen Curry’s wife Ayesha Curry also reflected on their marriage as she said, "That’s how we maintain a good marriage -- making sure that we put the relationship first, because when our relationship is happy and thriving, the kids are too," she said.The two share four children together and seem pretty happy even after close to two decades of being married to one another.All that the four time NBA champion Stephen Curry is focusing on now is how to bounce back on the court as the team battles tough injuries.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Fran Fraschilla on why he wrote a book, and previewing the 2026-27 college basketball season
articles.summary: College basketball’s regular season starts next month, and few people are more excited than Fran Fraschilla. The ESPN analyst and former coach is adding a ne...
articles.body:
College basketball's regular season starts next month, and few people are more excited than Fran Fraschilla.

The ESPN analyst and former coach is adding a new title to his résumé: author. Don't Mess With Happy will be released on Oct. 20 and is now available for pre-order. Co-written with David Smale , Fraschilla's new book features stories and lessons from two decades as a college coach and two decades as a broadcaster.

Fraschilla coached at Manhattan, St. John's, and New Mexico. He joined ESPN in 2003 and has not returned to coaching. We recently spoke with Fraschilla about his book and to preview the 2026-27 season.

Note: This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

Fran Fraschilla: "I coached for 23 years. I left at 43, thinking I was heading back after a hiatus. Once I got to ESPN, I decided, with two little boys living in Highland Park in Dallas, that I probably wouldn't mess with happy, and I stayed.

"It's a lifetime love affair with the game of basketball, which starts in Brooklyn, New York, as a city kid on the playgrounds, 23 years of coaching, and now going into my 24th year of broadcasting. I'm not necessarily the hero of the book. I'm just a guide to so many great basketball stories about people like Jay Wright, Tom Izzo, Rick Barnes, Brent Musburger, Jon Sciambi, and on. I've been in some unique places in basketball, and I decided to put it down on paper."

What would you consider the most fascinating detail in your book?

"I decided to go to Marquette University to be the associate head coach in 2007. It's the first chapter of the book. I was going to a place that had come off a Final Four (in 2003), with a Hall of Fame player in Dwyane Wade and a very close friend in Tom Crean. I was 90 minutes from getting on a plane in Dallas and going to Milwaukee, and I talked to my boss at ESPN. It was basically some niceties. He did a great job and said all the best of luck. As soon as I hung up the phone, I told my wife, I'm not messing with happy. I'm staying in broadcasting. That's the hook of the book, in the sense that here's a guy who could have easily gone back to coaching."

So, there was a sliding-doors situation where you could have been Marquette's head coach?

"The next year (Crean) leaves for Indiana, and the guy that he hired (as associate head coach) was Buzz Williams. When Tom left, Buzz became Marquette's head coach. The cool thing is, I haven't regretted my decision to stay in TV for a second because it's a great lifestyle. I'm still around the game. I'm around the game every day. I have been since I was 13, whether it's talking to coaches, doing coaching clinics, or putting out coaching videos. And ironically, because I stayed home to be a father, I have a son coaching in the NBA and a son coaching in the ACC . I'm not sure that would have happened had it not been for me being able to spend so much time with them when they were just little boys in Dallas."

Did you receive any other offers after turning down Marquette?

"I was offered the head coaching job at South Florida in the Big East… Later, Bobby Cremins tried to talk me into going to College at Charleston, a great mid-major job. I decided against it. I would have missed my son Matt's senior year of high school. And sure enough, he got an offer to play at Harvard for Tommy Amaker. My life's been idyllic in the sense that I've had two incredible careers."

Let's look ahead to the upcoming season. Today, who is the best team in college basketball?

"Hands down, it's Florida, because they have three guys on the frontline who are all capable of being on NBA rosters right now: Thomas Haugh, Alex Condon, and Rueben Chinyelu. They all decided to stay at Florida. They're probably getting paid well via NIL. For that reason, they're an anomaly in college basketball because they've chosen to stay together for one more year. All three of them won a national championship two years ago, so they're clearly the best team. I think Duke would probably be not far behind, along with UConn."

Do you think this will be Bill Self's final season at Kansas?

"Bill and I are very close, but we haven't talked about it. If they have a great season, which depends on how the judges rule on two key guys, Melvin Council Jr. and Tre White , I think it could be a really good year for Kansas. But I would bet this will be Bill Self's final year, in part because I think he wants to go out with a good team and a good taste in his mouth. He's accomplished everything in basketball. The one thing I do know about him, because I talked to him about this, is that he wants to be a really good grandfather. I say that not flippantly. …But I think Bill wants to really spend time making sure his health is great, that his golf game is better, and that he's a great grandfather. So, I would not be surprised if this is his final season."

Who is the best college basketball player?

"I would say on Jan. 1, it'll be JT Toppin when he comes back from his knee injury at Texas Tech. I think (Florida's) Thomas Haugh could make an argument. (Duke's) Joaquim Boumtje-Boumtje, Ruben Boumtje-Boumtje's son, will be 17. If he's not the best player in college basketball, he'll be in the top five. A sleeper player-of-the-year candidate would be Tyler Tanner at Vanderbilt, who turned down a chance to play in the NBA to come back. Another guy that, if he's healthy, is David Mirkovic at Illinois, who I love. People are just finding out how good he is."

What challenges will Michael Malone face at North Carolina?

"There's more coaching in one NBA game than there is in three college games because of the length of possessions and the fact that you're trying to stop the best players in the world.

"In-game coaching won't be an issue for Michael. It's all the stuff away from the court, the recruiting, the transfer portal, which is essentially the biggest part of recruiting right now, and the fact that he's going to spend less time coaching basketball than he would in the NBA, where all you do is coach basketball. So the adjustment is not going to be on the court. It's going to be how good a talent level they've been able to put together in the first year. From what I can see, they probably have top-20 talent, which is a good thing for a first-year head coach, especially one who got the job in April. But I think he's going to have to grow into the job as far as all the other things that go on in college."

Which non-power-conference team should we watch closely?

"VCU comes to mind. Phil Martelli Jr. has done a great job there. The A-10 has been somewhat underrated. Phil Jr. has a team that I think could really make noise in the postseason. I think College of Charleston can be a team (to watch) out of the CAA. John Groce has coached at Illinois. He had success at Ohio. Again, the transfer portal lets you get good players quickly. John put together, I think, a very good team there."

"No, but right off the top of my head, it's the upset of the season if Florida is not in the Final Four… I think Illinois, when they are fully healthy and get David Mirkovic back, and Michigan State are clearly Final Four-worthy. I think Arizona is Final Four-worthy. I think Duke is Final Four-worthy."

"I'll give you a couple of teams that might be on the fringe, and Virginia is one for sure. If you want a dark horse for the Final Four, I would say the Miami Hurricanes with Jai Lucas. If they get Malik Reneau reinstated and his eligibility restored, that is absolutely a team that, if they got to Detroit, you would not be shocked."

articles.title: College sports needs limits | Opinion
articles.summary: Senior Staff Writer Kayra Serpenguzel examines the Senate’s College Sports Bill and the implications for FSU athletes.
articles.body:
The Protect College Sports Act , created by Senator Ted Cruz and Maria Cantwell, passed the U.S. Senate to maintain national standards for college athletes. This bipartisan bill directly impacts the current NIL (Name, Image, and Likeness) framework, transfer rules, and eligibility requirements.

Yet while this bill instates limits on college athlete compensation and behavior such as transfers and years of eligibility, there are significant gaps this bill isn't addressing. The most imperative of these gaps are coaching pay and facility spending.

Coaching salaries in universities, especially for revenue-generating sports like football and basketball, can average millions of dollars. Division one coaches at the highest level are paid between 8 million and 13.3 million dollars annually.

Facilities for Division I sports are also expensive to maintain and build. The New York Times recently reported on a more than $100 million football indoor training facility at the University of Notre Dame. The Dunlap football center at FSU costs between $138 million and $150 million. There are also immense costs to upgrade facilities to give athletes better resources, as well as to maintain the facilities.

The U.S. Government Accountability Office reported that 94% of NCAA Division 1 athletic programs actually spend more money than they generate. The money necessary to fund these programs, coaches' salaries, and facilities then comes from general funds, taxes, and student fees.

There was initially a proposed amendment titled " Salary Cap for Coaches ," sponsored by Senators Cory Booker and Chris Murphy. The amendment would set a $5 million cap annually per coach. They argued that this bill only limits athlete compensation while leaving coaches with unlimited and unchecked salaries. This amendment failed in the U.S. Senate.

The proposed Senate amendment, if it had passed, would have affected approximately 40% of current coaching salaries for major varsity sports.

"I think that the fact that this bill only addresses the salaries of athletes and not coaches is reflective of the difference between a student-athlete and a professional coach. These athletes are students, primarily a student at that institution, while being a coach is solely a profession," said second-year international affairs major at FSU Ada Jones to the FSView.

Historically, coach compensation exceeds athlete compensation in the NCAA in this "arms race," a perspective agreed upon by Nick Saban , a former football coach for the University of Alabama.

Yet while this bill isn't addressing these major costs for Division 1 sports programs, there are important aspects that it will codify into law. One of the most important aspects of this bill is that athlete compensation will have required disclosures of deals over $600. Additionally, every college athlete is allowed only one "free" transfer, meaning they won't have to sit out that season. After the first transfer, there will be a season where the athlete can't compete in their sport.

"I agree with limiting portal transfers because there's no reason you should be able to go to a different school every year and not commit to the school because it shows a lack of loyalty and makes the school scramble to pay for different athletes, and I think that they would be more bound to their contract; they'd make smarter decisions to the school they commit to," said second-year political science major at FSU Emma Claire Goldstein to the FSView.

One of the sponsors of the bill, Senator Maria Cantwell , said that the PCSA "is about reining in the bad practices that are happening in college sports today, the runaway costs... [and] the runaway arms race in sports spending."

"Historically, college athletes have generated substantial commercial value for the institutions they play for, having limited participation in the profits of their hard work. Athletes deserve a meaningful share in that value," said Cannon Boyles, a second-year, to the FSView.

Through the PCSA, athletes will be given a maximum of 5 years to finish their college sports career, with no exceptions. While this rule is already codified in the NCAA , exceptions like medical waivers, an extra year due to the COVID-19 pandemic, financial incentives from NIL, and redshirt years push beyond the 5-year boundary.

Cam McCormick , a former college football player who was a tight end for the Oregon Ducks and Miami Hurricanes, was granted 9 years of eligibility. Although this is an extreme example, supporters of the bill believe that older athletes who are 27 and 28 years old shouldn't be competing against teenagers.

This bill also may have specific implications for Florida. Senator Rick Scott was one of two GOP "No" votes on the Protect College Sports Act, while Senator Moody voted "Yes" after an amendment on conference realignment. Their initial opposition was due to how, under the PCSA, schools in Big Three conferences like the ACC have to serve three years in probation if they want to switch conferences.

Redshirt years are specific periods where a college athlete doesn't play in official games and competitions to preserve a year of their athletic eligibility. The athlete still practices with their team, receives athletic scholarships, and attends classes.

There are also increased benefits for the athletes in the form of health and academic protections. The athletes will have 5 years of post–eligibility medical coverage for any injuries sustained because of their college sport. There will also be a 10-year degree completion guarantee, with the university honoring the scholarship given to the athlete so they can finish their education.

Another aspect of this bill is the Antitrust protections, which will now be extended to college sports. This bill will therefore give the NCAA and its member schools protection from lawsuits and freedom to set shared rules without being sued. This part of the bill directly addresses the recent House v. NCAA settlement, which established a $20.5 million revenue-sharing cap .

The House of Representatives previously had a similar bill, the Student Compensation and Opportunity through Rights and Endorsements (SCORE) Act, which has stalled twice. The main distinction between this legislation and the PCSA is that college athletes are not seen as employees of the university under the SCORE Act.

The bill is currently with the House of Representatives after it was passed by the Senate. The House isn't set to return until November 9, which is after the midterm election. The White House has expressed earnest support for this bill in a statement to "Save College Sports."

Kayra Serpenguzel is a Political Science and Creative Writing major at Florida State University and a Senior Staff Writer for the Views section of the FSView & Florida Flambeau, the student-run, independent online news service for the FSU community. Email our staff at contact@fsview.com .

articles.body:
The New York Knicks are reportedly expected to pursue a trade in order to make room for veteran guard Bruce Brown on their roster.

According to SNY's Ian Begley , there is "strong support" within the organization to keep Brown in the fold, and if the Knicks are going to do that, they must make a trade by Monday.

Begley expects the Knicks to "explore all avenues" in order to do so, and named Pacôme Dadiet and Tyler Kolek as the team's prime trade candidates.
